name: Total Depravity and the Bondage of the Will

objectives.text: Identify from Scripture that sin affects every part of a person, including the heart, thoughts, words, and actions
Recall that the Bible describes people apart from God as dead in their sins
Recall from Scripture that no one can save himself by being good enough
Describe what Genesis 6:5 and Jeremiah 17:9 teach about the natural condition of the human heart
Explain the Reformed meaning of total depravity as the corruption of every human faculty rather than people being as wicked as they could possibly be
Explain from Romans 8:7-8 why the natural person cannot please God
Compare the biblical picture of the sinner as spiritually dead with the idea that the sinner is merely sick or weak
Distinguish total depravity from utter depravity by explaining how unregenerate people can still perform outwardly good civil acts
Explain why the sinner's inability means that salvation must be entirely of God's grace
Explain the bondage of the will as the slavery of the fallen person to sin using the words of Jesus and Paul
Interpret Jeremiah 17:9 within its surrounding passage to explain what it teaches about self-deception and the heart
Analyze John 6:44 and 6:65 to show how spiritual inability prevents anyone from coming to Christ unless drawn by the Father
Explain the noetic effects of sin by describing from Scripture how sin darkens the mind's understanding of God
Distinguish the natural liberty of the will, which is not forced, from the moral inability of the fallen will to choose spiritual good
Describe the fourfold state of the human will in innocence, in sin, in grace, and in glory
Trace the historical debates over the will between Augustine and Pelagius and between Luther and Erasmus
Construct a biblical argument for human inability that draws on texts from both Testaments
Evaluate Pelagian, Semi-Pelagian, and Arminian accounts of free will against the Reformed doctrine of total depravity
Defend the doctrine of depravity against the claim that people are basically good using Scripture and reasoned argument
Analyze how total depravity functions as the foundation for the other doctrines of grace, such as unconditional election and effectual calling

changes: Kept real competencies (every part affected, dead in sin, cannot save oneself, natural heart, defining total depravity, cannot please God, sick versus dead, grace alone, bondage of the will, Jeremiah 17:9, John 6:44, noetic effects, argument for inability, evaluating free-will views, defending against basic goodness) and reworded them as observable student actions. Recast the grade 3 'observe' item as describing specific texts. Moved Jeremiah 17:9 interpretation to a contextual reading of verses 5-10. Dropped the vague grade 12 'dark backdrop' synthesis and replaced it with analysis of depravity's role among the doctrines of grace. Added total versus utter depravity with civil good, natural liberty versus moral inability, the fourfold state of the will, and the Augustine-Pelagius and Luther-Erasmus debates. Updated confession citations to full names and added WCF 6.4, 9.1-9.5, 10.1-10.2, 16.7, Heidelberg Q8, and Canons of Dort 3/4.1 and 3/4.4. Avoided origin, imputation, and consequences material that belongs to sibling sub-topics.
